notes: Trigger evaluation for an offered-not-requested skill. Positives deliberately NEVER mention Warp: the skill must fire on the problem shape (irregular/spatial/simulation hot path, iterative per-element loops, or many small kernels on NVIDIA hardware) because Warp is offered as a solution rather than named by the user. Negatives are gated cases the description must suppress: CPU-only or no-GPU deployment, required non-NVIDIA portability, dense tensor/NN work already served by vendor libraries, plain Warp API or packaging questions, and requests where the user has already chosen a Warp kernel and only wants it written. Query 23 is deliberately a positive even though the project already ships a GPU backend: an existing accelerator path is a codebase-level judgement for stage 1 and the baselines ladder, not something the description can screen on, and treating it as a description-level negative would suppress the skill on exactly the assessments it should run. No query names the skill or states a desired verdict. Split is fixed at 60/40 with a proportional positive/negative mix in each half. Queries 27-30 come from a full assessment of a library that ships hand-written CUDA for nearly every operation. 27 and 28 are positives that look like negatives: an operation that ALREADY has a maintained CUDA kernel is not a description-level negative (that kernel can still be the wrong algorithm - a mature implementation gate is a codebase judgement, and firing it from the description would suppress the assessment that discovers it), and neither is a project that supports a second vendor, so long as an optional NVIDIA path is acceptable - portability is a cost to price into the verdict, not a disqualifier, and query 15 stays a negative only because it REQUIRES parity across all three targets. 29 and 30 are negatives that look like positives: both describe irregular geometry work on real hardware, but neither states a latency, throughput, memory or capacity objective - one asks whether a tie-breaking difference is a bug and the other asks for cross-release determinism. Correctness and reproducibility are gates on a migration, never reasons for one, so the skill must not load to answer them. Queries 31-34 come from an assessment of a library of GPU operations whose packaging policy forbids runtime code generation. 31 and 32 are positives that are easy to mistake for negatives: 31 describes a deployment that cannot accept a runtime-compiled dependency, but that is a codebase/policy fact the description cannot see - suppressing the skill there would skip the stage-1 gate that is supposed to fire and produce the ABORT. 32 is a library maintainer with no application of their own, which is a normal target for this skill even though the user frames the ranking question around their own microbenchmark. 33 is a negative because it asks about Warp's release policy rather than about making code faster, and 34 is a negative because the operation is already on a vendor library and near the bandwidth roofline.

queries.query: our particle neighbour search is eating most of the frame budget in the sim. positions are already on the gpu as torch tensors. what are our options here?

broad-phase collision in our cloth solver is a python loop over grid cells and it's clearly the bottleneck. ideas for speeding it up?
We're standing up a signed-distance-field query service on H100s and scipy's KDTree falls over at 10M points. What should we be building this on?
Our contact solver is about forty small hand-written CUDA kernels and launch overhead is dominating on the RTX 6000. Two of the three people who understand it are leaving.
TSDF integration over 10 cameras OOMs on the intermediate tensors at 256^3. Everything's GPU-resident already. How do we get the memory down?
connected components over batched binary masks on the gpu — our torch version does a fixed 100 propagation passes and it's both slow and sometimes wrong on big blobs
We raycast 500k rays against a deforming mesh every frame and currently rebuild the BVH on the CPU each time. It's a CUDA box. This is killing our frame time.
got irregular per-element work with early exits over ~5M elements on an L40. vectorising it in torch materialises enormous mask tensors and we run out of memory
Our MD code rebuilds neighbour lists every step in JAX and allocates multi-gigabyte candidate tensors on the A100s. We want to run bigger systems.
our CLI ships to field engineers on laptops, no GPU anywhere in the fleet. the point-classification step is the slowest part of a run — can you speed it up?
score_batch is 71% of our p99 — four nn.Linear layers, a LayerNorm and a softmax, fp16 on A100s. We need that latency down.

our fp16 matmuls are slower than we expected on H100 — is that a BLAS choice, a layout problem, or are we just at the roofline?
panning our scatter dashboard over ~100M rows takes about 40 s a frame. the binning step is a per-row scatter with atomics and the dataframe already lives on the gpu. what are our options?

graph edge bundling takes 12 minutes on a 20k-edge graph. it's an iterative loop that nudges every point along a gradient field, 50 steps per round, and it's pure host code. anything better than waiting?
we already have numba.cuda kernels for the aggregation, but a post-processing pass in the same pipeline still runs on the host and now dominates the frame. where should we take this?
how do I get Warp's kernel cache working on a read-only container filesystem? it recompiles every start and I just need the cache path story.
our nightly pandas groupby over 50M rows takes 90 s on the managed Spark cluster. that cloud region has no GPU instance types available to us and procurement is closed.
we need bit-exact float64 geometry results reproducible across CPU, NVIDIA and AMD for a regulatory audit trail. currently the CPU path is the slow one.

the closest-point call in our geometry lib is already a hand-written CUDA kernel we've maintained for four releases, and it's still the top of every profile at scale. is there anything left in it or have we hit the hardware?

neighbourhood_features is basically all of our per-sweep time on the survey appliance and it looks like a textbook GPU workload. every unit has an A4000 in it that sits idle between classifier calls. what are our options?

we maintain a library of point-cloud and graph ops and we're deciding what to optimise next. our own per-op benchmark ranks them for us. putting a spatial index over the point positions is the obvious idea - is it worth it?
we're deciding whether to take warp-lang as an optional dependency in our library. what's its release cadence, how long do APIs stay supported, and does it follow semver?
our segmented reduction over 2M edges is the hot spot. it's already a single cusparse call and nsight says we're at about 85% of achievable bandwidth on the card. anything left here?
